To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
age‐related anabolism is blunted due to deficits in anabolic factors, and that this is underpinned by impaired translational efficiency.
age‐related deficits in muscle protein synthesis and anabolic hormones underlie the age‐related blunting of the hypertrophic response to resistance exercise training.
“Skeletal muscle protein synthesis and muscle ribosomal biogenesis are chronically impaired with age, and these deficits underlie age‐associated anabolic resistance to resistance exercise.”
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and metabolic adaptations to resistance exercise training (RET).
the mechanisms underlying age‐related changes in muscle protein turnover.
the mechanisms that underpin age‐related muscle wasting and the development of novel strategies to prevent and reverse this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

chronic deficits in long term muscle protein synthesis underpin age related exercise adaptation deficits and are likely to be the consequence of a multifactorial deficit in anabolic hormones, translational efficiency and ribosomal capacity.

age‐related anorexia of aging is a major factor contributing to the anabolic resistance to RET in older men, which is further compounded by a reduction in the translational efficiency and ribosome biogenesis.

the age‐related decline in muscle protein synthesis and anabolic hormones are the main contributors to age‐related muscle loss and that the age‐associated decline in muscle protein turnover is multifactorial.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
age‐related anabolism is impaired at all levels of translation.

we have demonstrated that the anabolic resistance to resistance exercise training with ageing is multifactorial, involving both reduced muscle protein synthesis rates and impaired ribosomal biogenesis.

age‐related anorexia of protein metabolism and anabolic resistance to RET are multifactorial and that the combination of anabolic resistance and anorexia are likely to underpin age‐related sarcopenia and the associated functional decline.
The main takeaway from our work is that
age‐related deficits in anabolic signalling and ribosomal biogeneration underlie the blunted muscle protein synthesis responses to RET in the elderly.
age‐related muscle protein synthesis deficits are multifactorial and that exercise and nutritional interventions are likely to be required to overcome these deficits.
older individuals are not as responsive to exercise training as their younger counterparts, but they can still benefit from exercise training.
